title: How secure are the space services Britain relies on?
label: 16 November 2026 · Space and national security
summary: Witnesses told the committee that British forces depend heavily on satellites to see, communicate and navigate, and could fight much less effectively if those services were disrupted or withheld. They discussed threats from Russia and China, dependence on allies and commercial providers, and ways to make access more reliable. They agreed that government needs to give industry clearer plans, but differed on whether national security equipment should be bought only from allies.

speakers.label: Dr Michelle Howard
speakers.name: Dr Michelle Howard
speakers.role: Defence and Space Policy Advisor at The D Group and Head of Defence at Space4Earth Capital

speakers.label: Nathan Mathiot
speakers.name: Nathan Mathiot
speakers.role: Director of Policy and Public Affairs at ADS Group, which represents aerospace, defence, security and space companies

speakers.label: Major General Paul Tedman
speakers.name: Major General Paul Tedman
speakers.role: Former Commander of UK Space Command and Managing Director for European Space at Anduril Industries

glossary.definition: A satellite-based system that provides location and timing information.
SpaceX’s military satellite communications service, described in the hearing as part of Starlink.
Military capabilities intended to protect access to space services and respond to threats against them.
In-orbit servicing and manufacturing: repairing, maintaining or making equipment in space.

chapters.title: What happens when satellites fail?
chapters.takeaway: Satellites help armed forces see, communicate and navigate, but access to those services cannot be taken for granted.

turns.speaker: Helen Maguire
turns.text: Which dependence on space-based equipment worries you most for our armed forces?

evidence.quote: What is the most concerning dependence that you feel that our Armed Forces have on space-based infrastructure?

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: Reliable access to communications and satellite images worries me. Russia disrupted Ukraine’s satellite internet at the start of its invasion, affecting military command. In March 2025, the US suspended Ukraine’s access to satellite imagery used to track Russian troops.

evidence.quote: the first act of war in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine was to disrupt and cyber attack Viasat’s satellite broadband internet access, thus disrupting Ukrainian command and control for the entire invasion.

In March 2025, the US suspended Ukrainian access to geospatial intelligence capabilities, thus disrupting their access to commercial satellite imagery platforms, Maxar Technologies. This stopped them being able to track Russian troop movements.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: I’m also concerned about relying on a company’s service. In October, SpaceX imposed speed restrictions on Starshield, which Ukraine used for military communications. I believe that badly affected its ability to communicate with drones.

evidence.quote: In mid-October this year, without warning SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starshield, which is the military grade satellite comms infrastructure part of Starlink.
This essentially stops the Ukrainian military’s ability to interact and communicate with its drones, and so obviously it has left them quite defenceless.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Without space services, forces lose much of their ability to see what’s happening, find their position, communicate and fight. We usually assume those services will be there.

evidence.quote: we just assume space capabilities are available to the land, maritime and air environments—you would not be able to understand through space-based ISR; you would not be able to move through positioning, navigation and timing; you would not be able to communicate through satellite communications and data relays; and, ultimately, you would not be able to fight.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: The UK also needs a reliable way to launch replacement satellites and restore services if they’re lost. That’s a particular concern for the future.

evidence.quote: we need to have assured access to launch, so we are able to replenish as part of the picture.
Beyond that, it is the challenge of how we then replenish those services. I think it is a particular concern for the UK going forward.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: If Britain lost access to its own or American space services, how well could its forces fight? And won’t plans for more automated equipment make that dependence greater?

evidence.quote: How prepared are British forces to fight were we to lose access to our own or American space services?
Does that not increase our dependence on space and thus our vulnerability should those systems be disrupted by either an adversary or a kill switch from an ally?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: They could still fight with maps and compasses, but not nearly as efficiently or effectively. Around 3,000 systems in an Army brigade rely on space. And yes, greater use of automated equipment increases the dependence.

evidence.quote: I think we will always be prepared to fight without space, going back to maps and compasses, but would we be efficient and effective? No. It is a simple answer, if you consider that 3,000 systems in an Army brigade rely on space-based systems.
Yes is the short answer

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: We need to ask two things: can we discourage an attack on those services, and, if one happens, can we absorb it while still giving our forces what they need? I can’t confidently answer yes.

evidence.quote: Do we have, first, the control and the capabilities to deter, and, secondly, should that deterrence fail—arguably we are close—are we resilient enough to be able to take a first-move punch, absorb it and still deliver those capabilities that are essential for our Armed Forces on the backside?
It is not a clear yes, Lord Sedwill.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: The defence plans set out what’s wanted and how to fund it. My worry is whether we can deliver it quickly enough to keep up with the growing threat.

evidence.quote: I would say that the SDR provides good ends—the strategy—and the DIP closes with the means. It is the ways that I worry about. Are we going to get there sufficiently quickly to match the threat?
That is the bit that I am worried about: time.

chapters.title: Depending on allies without losing control
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said Britain cannot quickly replace allied systems, but should secure greater control over the services and equipment it needs.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: The planned armed forces will share more information and use more automated systems, all of which makes them more dependent on space. Losing space services wouldn’t stop them overnight, but it would gradually reduce how far, fast and accurately they could operate.

evidence.quote: this means that it is definitely more networked and it is autonomous, which requires space-based assets. So, yes, we are a lot more dependent.

It would not stop our capability overnight, but it would progressively reduce our range for deep precision strike, tempo, precision, awareness, connectivity, and our operational integration across all five domains.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: So does dependence on space put the whole plan to modernise the armed forces at risk if those services fail?

evidence.quote: it sounds as though what you are saying is that, sitting behind the entire SDR strategy of modernising the force, the digital targeting web, integrated capability and hybrid capability, is, in effect, a single point of failure, which is a dependence on space-based technology in order to enable all of that. Or am I overstating it?

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: I wouldn’t quite put it that way, but achieving the effectiveness promised by that plan relies heavily on space—perhaps more heavily than people realise.

evidence.quote: I do not want to say that you are overstating it but the ability to be as effective as we would like to be, as defined in that strategy, is heavily reliant on space in a way that is perhaps not appreciated.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: Britain can’t make every component or service itself, and it will rely heavily on allies, especially the US, for years. The practical question is how to keep secure, consistent access. For example, Britain could retain the ability to approve software changes to its equipment without seeking permission abroad, and maintain local manufacturing so it can replace equipment after an attack.

evidence.quote: It is not in our gift to have entirely sovereign supply chains and sovereign capability, but what we are really asking is: how do we assure consistent and secure access to the capabilities that we acquire?

so that, in order to update software in weapon systems, you do not have to go to a foreign country to request permission for that software update and can continue to use that platform; and localised IP manufacturing facilities so that we can reconstitute locally in the case of an attack.
We will heavily rely on allied assistance for many years to come, in particular from the US

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Are we also dependent on technology from countries outside our close group of allies?

evidence.quote: Are we dependent, for example, on Chinese technology—on technology from outside the close group of countries with which we work?

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: This isn’t my area of expertise, but chips and rare earth minerals used in important systems do come from non-allies. We need more work tracing suppliers before we can understand the full risk.

evidence.quote: It is not my area of expertise, but I know that, obviously, the microprocessor chips, semiconductors and rare earth minerals that go into our critical systems are certainly supplied by non-allies. But there is a whole level of supply chain provenance work that needs to be done in order to really understand the full extent of our vulnerabilities there.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: Government and industry need a longer-term relationship. Rather than mainly giving grants for research, government should gradually buy working equipment and services over time. That would give companies a steadier customer and help keep the UK industry strong.

evidence.quote: There is a need for a more mature, strategic relationship between the two sides.

there has been a bit of an overreliance and tendency towards offering grant funding towards the sector in the R&D space. There is a need to transition over time, not abruptly, towards more procurement of capability as a long-term customer to sustain a more robust industrial base as a whole.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: Different needs call for different choices: Britain may need to control some services itself, secure dependable access to others, and buy others from trusted partners or the commercial market. Working with allies such as Japan could stretch a limited budget, though it creates dependencies too.

evidence.quote: There are things we clearly might want to have under sovereign control, there are things we might want to have assured access to and there are things we might want to buy from trusted partners. There are also things we might be quite happy to get from the commercial market

working with allies like Japan, for example, where we can make our limited budget—if we are being honest—go much further, notwithstanding the point that, of course, there are certain tensions in terms of dependencies that this can also introduce into the mix.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Can technology solve problems such as fake or blocked GPS signals, or will those attacks remain possible however much we spend?

evidence.quote: is there a practical, technical solution to some of these vulnerabilities? Is this a question of throwing enough resources at it to ensure assured access to GPS, communications, or whatever it might be, or is it simply the case that there is no technical solution that can avoid the spoofing, jamming and other disruptive techniques?

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: I’m not the technical expert to settle that. I don’t think there’s one fix: options being explored include ground-based alternatives to satellite navigation and using different satellite providers. Having several ways to provide a service could make an attacker less confident of knocking it out.

evidence.quote: I am not going to be the technical expert to offer an informed view on that.

I am not sure if this is something that boils to down to one singular capability area that we need to take in-house, or we need to harden and make resilient, or we need to provide a terrestrial alternative.
we are exploring terrestrial solutions. We are exploring how we work with Eutelsat OneWeb in offering a diversity of options
This will thereby raise the level of uncertainty for our adversaries that they can have a decisive impact

chapters.title: Threats that are no longer theoretical
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses described several ways satellites can be disrupted or attacked, and said space’s importance is still not widely understood.

turns.speaker: Lord Godson
turns.text: What threats do Russia, China and others pose in space? And do the public and government understand those threats well enough?

evidence.quote: I would like to hear from all of you on your views on that. We have rightly heard about Russia specifically, but I would also like to hear more about China and other sorts of threats
your view of the success of government in educating both the public and indeed Whitehall and the other services—services in the wider sense—about these threats.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: The threats range from temporarily blocking signals to grabbing satellites or firing missiles at them. Russia has stated an intention to put a nuclear weapon in orbit. Most, if not all, of these types of capability have been demonstrated; they aren’t science fiction.

evidence.quote: people generally talk to a continuum from non-kinetic reversible jamming, just disruption of space capabilities, all the way through to exo-atmospheric nuclear explosions on orbit. In between, there are capabilities that can grapple other satellites. There are direct ascent anti-satellite missiles that launch from terrestrial sites into orbit. Most, if not all, of those capabilities have been demonstrated and are real. Russia has put a stated intent out that it wishes to put a nuclear weapon on orbit
That range of capabilities is not science fiction any more

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: In my view, China has more sophisticated space capabilities but is more predictable in its decisions. Russia has less capability but has acted in ways we didn’t expect. Together, they’re a serious problem; their equipment for disrupting or attacking space services has grown considerably since 2021.

evidence.quote: China is far more sophisticated in its capabilities on orbit, but is more of a rational actor
Russia has less capability but is irrational. The two together pose us a problem. But they have increased their counterspace arsenal by 70% since 2021 as two nations

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Space specialists can argue for more attention, but it carries more weight when senior military leaders explain why they need space services. Defence has added space and cyber operations to its responsibilities without a corresponding rise in the overall budget.

evidence.quote: space people advocating for space only gets you so far.
when the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff stood up and said that our most important domain is space, people started paying attention.
We have kept the same broad defence budget but increased to five domains. There is a challenge within defence and wider government in integrating space into our thinking.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: There’s a long way to go with the public too. In a recent UK survey, 21% of people first associated space with aliens, while only 8% thought of communications and connectivity. Rockets and astronauts attract interest; explaining the less exciting services we use every day is harder.

evidence.quote: the first word that 21% of the UK public associated with space was “aliens” and only 8% thought about communications and connectivity.
it is quite difficult to demonstrate the integral nature of our UK space capabilities without being inherently boring. The things that really inspire people are the astronauts and the rocket launches

chapters.title: What government should buy—and from whom
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses wanted clearer government purchasing plans, but named different priorities and disagreed over buying only from allies.

turns.speaker: Lord Watts
turns.text: What should government do to help defence space companies, and which services should it spend public money on first?

evidence.quote: What more can the Government do to support companies in the defence sector to be more resilient and to improve the security of the products, and which space-based systems and services should the Government be looking to prioritise for public expenditure?

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: Companies need to see how much government expects to spend each year and what it plans to buy. That would give them confidence to invest in the UK. My priority is the ability to launch satellites: the UK and Europe depend too much on existing launch capacity, including SpaceX.

evidence.quote: we need that year-by-year breakdown of the pipeline to encourage investment in resilient capabilities.

I would pick out launch capability as a particular area where we can see that there is a bottleneck in existing dependence, for example, on SpaceX capacity. The UK and Europe as a whole need to strengthen their own launch capabilities.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: Government should be clear about what it wants and publish a dependable schedule of contracts. I wouldn’t prescribe every spending priority, but ISAM—servicing and manufacturing equipment in orbit—is an area where the UK has a real strength.

evidence.quote: Clear strategic intent and a contract pipeline would be the best thing Government could do to support our defence space industrial base.

I dare not say which, although ISAM—in-orbit servicing and manufacturing—is a real area of strategic strength for us. It is worth Government leaning into that and developing and focusing on those capabilities.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Government also needs to make clear who’s in charge of space policy and speed up how it buys equipment. For capability, I’d prioritise space control: the plans already identify it as an area where Britain isn’t investing enough.

evidence.quote: very clear leadership from Government about who is in charge would be super helpful.
There is a lot of work to do in procurement and acquisition reform.
the capability we are underinvesting in is space control.

turns.speaker: Lord Watts
turns.text: Should Britain buy national security equipment only from allies?

evidence.quote: do you think we should procure only from our allies?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: No. We should diversify our suppliers without cutting ourselves off from our closest allies in space.

evidence.quote: No, it is both. I think we need to diversify but not divorce from our closest allies in space.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: Yes. For national security equipment, we should buy only from allies.

evidence.quote: Yes, we should procure national security assets only from our allies.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: I agree with Michelle on buying from allies.

evidence.quote: Yes, the same as Michelle.
